Interviewer: This is a United States Holocaust Memorial Museum interview with Mrs. Floor Eva Miller, on May 5th, 2013, in Brooklyn, New York. Thank you Mrs. Miller for agreeing to meet with us today, for agreeing to tell your story, and we will start at the beginning. So I’d like you to tell me when you were born, your date of birth, where you were born, and your name at birth.
Interviewee: Okay, I was born in January 17, 1928, and it was Rad w, Poland. My name is Flora Eva, my maiden name. And that’s as far as I remember my birth, and being — I mean, growing up — excuse me, growing up with two brothers older than I, and my father —
Interviewer: Tell me — okay, excuse me.
Interviewee: — my mother.
Interviewer: Tell me their names and when they were born.
Interviewee: My oldest brother was Burhman Eva. He was born in 1923, I don’t remember the date. And my middle brother was born in 1925, in July of 1925. Also in the same town as myself in Poland, and we all attended — later on we attended I — a grade school, which is in Polish, you know. Every — every Jewish child, no matter what religion they was, Orthodox, or very Orthodox, had to attend seventh grade in Polish school. And if the parents could allow themselves, they also sent the children to Hebrew schools, and that’s where I attended after public school: after lunch from one to five, we attended Hebrew school.
Interviewer: So you had a long day.
Interviewee: And — yes. And also my brothers attended, learning everything, Judaism and religious and every — we were religious, we were very Orthodox at home. But the kids, you know, my father was *** he is sending his boys, his sons to learn whatever is needed to be learned, until the war broke out.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: I finished my fourth grade just in 1939, and we also finished some of the Hebrew school, not everything, because the war started. And then the Germans came in —
Interviewer: Hang on a minute, hang on a minute.
Interviewee: Okay.
Interviewer: We’ll get there. But in the beginning I’d like to ask you many more questions about your childhood, about growing up, about pre-war life. So —
Interviewee: Like what?
Interviewer: About life before the war.
Interviewee: The war?
Interviewer: So first I’d like to ask, beca — to make sure that we have it on record, your middle brother’s name, your — the one born in 1925, what is it?
Interviewee: ***
Interviewer: Your older brother is Pinkhus or —
Interviewee: Burhman, yeah.
Interviewer: Yes. And your younger brother?
Interviewee: My — is Jacques.
Interviewer: Jacques. Jacques was his name.
Interviewee: Yeah, Jacques. We call him Jackie, because he has two names, Jacques Jackie.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: And what were your father’s name and your mother’s maiden name?
Interviewee: Matej Eva was my father, and my mother’s name was Louise Eva.
Interviewer: Louise Eva. ***
Interviewee: Born Garcia.
Interviewer: Born Garcia.
Interviewee: Yeah, married to Eva.
Interviewer: Were your parents from Rozwadow?
Interviewee: Yes.
Interviewer: So their families —
Interviewee: They were both — they both born in Rozwadow. Officially their parents were born not directly in Rozwadow, but one of the towns near Rozwadow. But when they got older, they all moved to Rozwadow. My grandfather was not a poor man, he had some business established, sh-shoe business *** business, and that’s what he learned his sons, like my father, my uncles. And my mother’s family, they were also living in Rozwadow, the Garcia family, and my grandfather was in business with agriculture, fish, fruits, all that, and he raised *** in Rozwadow. And they all did get married in Rozwadow.
Interviewer: So —
Interviewee: The siblings of my mother, and the siblings of my father.
Interviewer: Do you remember your mother’s and father’s birthdates?
Interviewee: My father’s birthday?
Interviewer: Mm-hm.
Interviewee: Yes, I remember, 1895.
Interviewer: 1895.
Interviewee: I don’t know the date.
Interviewer: It’s okay. And your mother’s?
Interviewee: Two years later, ’97.
Interviewer: In 1897.
Interviewee: 1897.
Interviewer: And would you say that your family was well-to-do, or —
Interviewee: Middle class.
Interviewer: Middle class.
Interviewee: Middle class. Not well-to-do, but middle class.
Interviewer: Uh-huh. And your father was in the shoe business?
Interviewee: No, my grandfather was in the shoe business. My father was going — when I already knew what he was doing. First he work with his father, of course, then he got married. And then he was going — I don’t know how you call it, he adjust the top of the shoes.
Interviewer: Ah, not the soles, but the uppers.
Interviewee: Not the whole shoe. Upper.
Interviewer: Uppers.
Interviewee: Right.
Interviewer: He was making uppers.
Interviewee: Only the upper, the leather, whatever —
Interviewer: Yeah.
Interviewee: — is needed for winter, for summer. And he developed his own business. My mother, of course, helped him when there was the season. And he had customers coming from the villages every Tuesday to order, you know, whatever they needed for their stores or for their families, whatever. My father worked very hard. And then, I grew up like every child, you know. Happy, hel —
Interviewer: Were you the youngest?
Interviewee: I was the youngest. I had friends, I was going to school, I was going to Hebrew school. Never have time too much to be outside like running around or whatever, because my father made sure that we should get whatever education we — we can.
Interviewer: So your father emphasized education.
Interviewee: Yeah, this was his first thing.
Interviewer: Was he himself educated?
Interviewee: As far as I know, he finished high school.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: So did my mother, but this was al-already in — not in Polish time, this was in *** time. That was under ger — under Austrian occupation.
Interviewer: Ah, I wou — I was gon —
Interviewee: And th — before the — the first war.
Interviewer: So that was my next question, because I’m not familiar with Polish geography.
Interviewee: Yeah.
Interviewer: I wanted to know where is Rozwadow in Poland. Is it in the west, in the center —
Interviewee: It’s in Galicia.
Interviewer: It’s in Galicia?
Interviewee: Galicia belonged to Austria, and then they gave it back to Poland —
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: — after the war in 1918.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: After the war finished. It was actually Poland before, but then occupied as Prince David, the King of Austria, he occupied the all Galicia, all the Ukraine, until the liberation of the first war, and then was Poland again.
Interviewer: Did your parents talk about the first World War —
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: — and any experiences they might have?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: No.
Interviewee: No, they never did.
Interviewer: They never did.
Interviewee: I have never talked to my children about what I went through.
Interviewer: What was life like at home? Was it — was your father and mother, were they strict, were they —
Interviewee: Well, he — he wanted the boys, mostly the boys to be very religious and have a good education, as far as he could afforded to pay for it.
Interviewer: And your mother, what was she —
Interviewee: My mother was *** she raised the children, she made whatever she could clothes. She was sewing clothes for myself, not for my brothers, just for me. She had a sister-in-law, which was a terrific dressmaker, so she used to cut material, and my mother used to sew it. So I always had nice clothes to go to school, or to go to friends, or as you could see from the picture, I was dressed like a middle class person, like a middle class child actually.
Interviewer: Was a middle class child in Poland, a middle class family, the same thing as in the United States?
Interviewee: No, poorer.
Interviewer: Poorer. Poorer.
Interviewee: Much poorer.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: A middle class family — I consider my son middle class, but we never could afforded what he has here, never.
Interviewer: Okay, did your parents own your own home — their own home?
Interviewee: They owned an apartment, yes, which consisted of two rooms and a kitchen. And of course a yard, and — and also *** shed where they kept, you know, stuff for the winter. And —
Interviewer: Did you have animals?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: Like no horses, no —
Interviewee: No, no.
Interviewer: Nothing like that.
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: Did you have a ma — an automobile?
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: Okay.
Interviewee: No.
Interviewer: How large was Rozwadow? Was it a big town?
Interviewee: The apartment are big?
Interviewer: No, no, the town. Rozwadow.
Interviewee: The town — we had — the town was not big
